idiom_name: Azure Service Bus dead-letter subqueue: ServiceBusProcessor + DeadLetterMessageAsync / MaxDeliveryCount
implementation_notes: .NET code does not build a dead-letter queue; it configures the one the messaging service already has. On Azure Service Bus every queue and subscription has a dead-letter subqueue: let the delivery count run out (MaxDeliveryCount, 10 by default) for transient failures, or call DeadLetterMessageAsync(message, reason, description) when the handler can prove the failure is permanent. The reason and description become the triage surface - system reasons include MaxDeliveryCountExceeded and TTLExpiredException - so use a stable classification plus the exception text. NServiceBus and MassTransit name the same idea differently ('error queue', `_error` queue), but the structure is this pattern; the alternative to the Azure mechanism is a framework error queue plus the broker's dead-letter exchange on RabbitMQ.
pitfalls: Peek-lock is required: in receive-and-delete mode the message is already gone and DeadLetterMessageAsync cannot park it.

Settling after the receiver is closed has no effect - the settlement never reaches the service, the lock expires, and the message eventually arrives in the DLQ as MaxDeliveryCountExceeded by accident rather than by decision.
The DLQ is a subqueue of the same entity and cannot be created, deleted or capacity-managed independently, so its backlog has to be drained deliberately or it accumulates forever.

Reason and description should be a stable classification plus exception type, not a raw stack trace: they are the only triage key the operator has, and oversized descriptions count against the message quota.
